entry.evidence: This episode was unique, however, in terms of its monotonic infrasonic spectra (consisting of a single peak in the frequency domain).

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text), with PDF for figures

steps.action: Report the anomaly: before lava fountain episode #4, the fundamental tone of monotonic infrasound glided from 0.7 to 3 Hz over about 24 h.
steps.quote: the fundamental tone of the monotonic infrasound rose from 0.7 Hz to 3 Hz in a pattern referred to as spectral gliding

steps.action: Take from the literature the candidate mechanisms for harmonic and gliding signals: conduit or bubble resonance, Helmholtz or crater resonance, repeating pulses, complex source functions, and magma rise in a resonating conduit.
steps.quote: Infrasonic gliding has been modeled as due to the rise or fall of magma within a resonating conduit

steps.action: State the aim: understand the source of the gliding and build a quantitative model of magma column position, velocity and volume over time.
steps.quote: to better understand the source of infrasonic gliding and to develop a quantitative model of magma column rise (position, velocity, and volume) over time

steps.action: Select 36 h of infrasound and seismic records from the INGV permanent network, compute spectrograms, and divide the pre-eruptive activity into three phases.
steps.quote: we focused on 36 h of infrasonic and seismic data from 19 February at 12:00 to 21 February at 00:00 UTC

steps.action: Locate the infrasound events and tremor windows by network grid search (brightness and semblance functions) and place the vast majority at SEC rather than BN.
steps.quote: This analysis confirms that the vast majority of discrete events and tremor were located at SEC

steps.action: Estimate the location uncertainty by jackknife (leaving one station out per run) and keep events with uncertainty below 250 m (Methods).
steps.quote: Uncertainty in the locations was estimated by the jackknife technique54

steps.action: Separate the volcanic signal from the ocean microbarom by network coherence, and exclude phase 2, where the microbarom dominates.
steps.quote: The microbarom is distinguishable from the volcanic signal as it is incoherent across the network

steps.action: Compare the infrasound with thermal imagery (EMOT camera) and co-located seismic records: gliding ends at the 19:00 Strombolian onset and is absent from the seismic data.
steps.quote: there is minimal seismic signal with no distinct spectral character prior to the start of Strombolian activity at 19:00

steps.action: Hypothesize a shallow subaerial source at the top of the magma column, resonating in the open crater/conduit and coupling to the atmosphere but not the ground.
steps.quote: we suspect that the source was subaerial and located very shallow (at the top of the magma column)

steps.action: Check that the gliding and the peak frequency are the same at every analysed station.
steps.quote: This infrasonic gliding observation was common to the signals acquired by all the analyzed infrasonic stations

steps.action: Exclude propagation, site and topographic-scattering effects as the cause of the gliding, given the consistency across stations.
steps.quote: likely indicative of a source process rather than changing propagation conditions

steps.action: Model the gliding as acoustic resonance of a crater/conduit whose length shortens as magma rises, with the closed-open pipe relation f = c/(4L) as a first approximation.
steps.quote: [...] model the gliding monotonic infrasound signal as an acoustic resonance of the crater and conduit

steps.action: Compare the timing of the highest peak frequencies with the explosions that became visible after 19:00, as support for a high magma column.
steps.quote: This supports the hypothesis that the magma column was high within the crater/conduit at this time.

steps.action: Reconstruct the SEC crater and conduit geometry from a 3 March UAS structure-from-motion DEM, aligned to the 2014 DEM, and fit a quasi-1D axisymmetric profile along the N-S transect.
steps.quote: Visual observations of the SEC and structure-from-motion mapping efforts reveal a shallow 65-m-radius crater sloping down towards a vertical conduit

steps.action: Check the UAS geometry against Sentinel-2 images from 18 and 23 February and 3 March, and against earlier SEC surveys, to estimate the geometry during the episode (Methods).
steps.quote: The satellite data were used to constrain the dimensions of the outer crater rim and confirm the results of the UAS survey.

steps.action: Use CRes to compute the acoustic response and peak frequency for magma depths from 300 to 50 m, assuming a constant 200 °C crater air temperature, an impulse source, and a -7.5 °C atmosphere.
steps.quote: We use CRes to simulate the acoustic response function for sources located at the bottom of SEC

steps.action: Compare the quasi-1D CRes results with 3D modelling to check CRes as a predictor for this crater.
steps.quote: a comparison of CRes results with 3D modeling confirming this is provided in Methods

steps.action: Test how sensitive the depth inversion is to model choice, topography, source spectrum and conduit temperature (supplement).
steps.quote: We consider the effects of four primary assumptions including model choice, uncertainty in topographic terrain, source spectrum, and conduit temperature.

steps.action: Invert the observed peak frequency at each time and station into magma depth through the CRes frequency-depth relation: about 170 m down to 78 ± 8 m, accelerating after 15:00.
steps.quote: This is modeled as a depth decrease from 167 ± 25 m to 138 ± 19 m over nine hours

steps.action: Invert the same frequencies with the cylindrical-pipe Eq. (1) (c = 436 m/s): depths are about 30 m shallower and show the same accelerating ascent.
steps.quote: Despite this simplified geometry, the inverted depths using Eq. (1) are qualitatively similar to the CRes results (~ 30 m shallower)

steps.action: Interpret the disappearance of the monotonic signal after 19:00 as the magma reaching the flaring crater, where conduit resonance is no longer sustained.
steps.quote: We attribute the loss of resonance to the magma level reaching the flaring crater of SEC where open conduit resonance is no longer sustained.

steps.action: Smooth and differentiate the inverted depths to estimate ascent velocity, then multiply by the cross-sectional area to estimate volumetric ascent rate, noting the sensitivity to conduit radius.
steps.quote: [...] moving median with a sliding window of 2 h to smooth the inverted depths and then differentiate

steps.action: Compare the gliding with the Villarrica 2015 precursor and with Spina et al.'s analogue degassing experiments.
steps.quote: Our interpretations are supported by the results obtained in Spina et al.42, who performed analogue degassing experiments

steps.action: Propose why only episode #4 glided: earlier large discharges drained the conduit, and later crater collapse prevented resonance (stated as speculation).
steps.quote: We speculate that these large discharges drained magma from the conduit so that prior to episode #4 the magma level was deep in the conduit

steps.action: Compare the ascent and volumetric rates with Villarrica (Johnson et al.) and with petrological and geophysical ascent-rate estimates (Petrelli et al.).
steps.quote: Infrasound-derived depths of the magma surface hint at a mean ascent rate of 5 m/hr and a maximum rate of 22 m/hr.

steps.action: Keep the claim that infrasound, resonance modelling and topography together constrain magma depth, ascent velocity and volumetric flux at high temporal resolution.
steps.quote: we place quantitative constraints on the magma depth, its ascent velocity and volumetric flux

steps.action: Refine the approach into a real-time monitoring option that uses the simple closed-open pipe model in place of CRes.
steps.quote: we demonstrate that the simple analytical model of an open-closed pipe can be used to produce qualitatively similar results

steps.action: Pose open questions for forecasting: when gliding occurs, the probability of a fountain after gliding, and a depth-based forecasting model.
steps.quote: In order for infrasonic gliding to be used as a forecasting tool, future work is needed

tree.answer: Yes: about 20-24 h of infrasonic gliding (0.7 to 3 Hz) before episode #4.
No: magma level is latent, inferred from peak frequency through an acoustic forward model.
Estimate magma column depth, ascent velocity and volume flux over time.
Literature mechanisms are listed; only source versus propagation/site effects is explicitly weighed.
Partly: propagation effects would differ by station; resonance predicts a monotonic frequency-depth relation.
Conditions found: a live eruption recorded by the permanent network.

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: No: gliding occurred in only 1 of 52 episodes; the analogue is Villarrica.
Yes: consistent across five stations, the Eq. (1) inversion, and sensitivity tests.
Kept: depth trajectory with stated uncertainties, plus ascent rates.
No review file supplied; two anonymous reviewers are only acknowledged.

end.claim: The infrasonic gliding records the magma column rising from about 172 ± 25 m to 78 ± 8 m below the crater rim over 24 h before the 20 February 2021 lava fountain.

decisive_move.sentence: Inverting each station's observed peak frequency through the CRes frequency-depth relation turns the gliding into a magma-depth time series.

gates.evidence: The data come from the permanent INGV monitoring network, and the UAS survey was flown after the event, so no hypothesis directed acquisition (§4.3 ¶1, §4.2 ¶4). The depth claim was checked against an independent simpler model (§2.5 ¶3), station-to-station consistency (§2.2 ¶9) and eruption timing (§2.3 ¶1); these checks were post hoc rather than a test that could fail. Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Resonance of a closed-open pipe, f = c/(4L), and acoustic impedance contrast
Structure-from-motion reconstruction with Agisoft Metashape from UAS imagery

novelty_claims.quote: Our featured example at Etna is the clearest example of infrasonic spectral gliding that we have seen reported.
This result represents one of the first examples of using infrasound to constrain magma rise rates leading to an eruption.

limits:
No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded; the acknowledgements mention two anonymous reviewers. The supplement was not supplied, so the temperature-sensitivity, source-function and four-assumption uncertainty analyses are coded on the authors' word.

The CRes versus 3D comparison is said to be 'provided in Methods', but the Methods text does not contain it (inference: it is in the supplement or was dropped).

The crater geometry rests on a survey flown on 3 March, after the crater changed shape. The 20 February geometry was estimated by comparison with satellite images, a step that carries no quantified uncertainty. Crater air temperature is assumed (200 °C), with no direct constraint.

Only one of 52 episodes showed gliding, so nature gives no repetition. Multi-station consistency was coded as robustness rather than replication, because all stations record the same single event; on this coding triangulation is not reached.

Sub-claims and their statuses:
- Loss of resonance at 19:00 because magma reached the crater flare: best_explanation.
- Shallow subaerial source and exclusion of propagation effects: best_explanation.
- Ascent velocity and volumetric flux: estimate_with_resolution, but radius-sensitive with unquantified uncertainty.
- Why only episode #4 glided (drained conduit, later collapse): explicitly speculative; status none.
- Real-time use of Eq. (1): capability_characterized for this geometry only.

Internal inconsistencies in the text:
- Starting depth: 172 ± 25 m (abstract) versus 170 ± 25 m (§2.5 ¶2).
- Volumetric rates: maximum 6300 versus 6200 m3/hr, and mean 1800 versus 1450 m3/hr (§2.5 ¶5, §3.2 ¶2).
- Episode #4 date: '22 February' in §4.2 ¶4 versus 20 February elsewhere.

An independent geodetic check was not possible: inflation was seen at a single tiltmeter only (§3.2 ¶4). The excitation mechanism is explicitly left to future work. Rival mechanisms are listed from the literature but not each tested.

disagreements.target: Petrelli et al. and references therein: basaltic ascent rates from petrological, thermal, mechanical and seismic methods
disagreements.support: Infrasound-derived rates are lower; the authors explain this by bulk-magma versus crystal movement and by open-conduit versus dyke settings.
disagreements.quote: Our ascent rates are mainly lower than the range of ascent rates (10–2–102 m/s) of basaltic melts inferred from methods

disagreements.target: Johnson et al. (2018), Villarrica magma ascent from infrasound
disagreements.support: That study gave depth only, from a single station, with a frequency change an order of magnitude smaller; this study adds ascent rate and flux from five stations.
disagreements.quote: While Johnson et al.19 calculated the depth to the magma column, they did not explicitly calculate the ascent rate or the volumetric flux.

disagreements.target: Watson et al. (2020), Etna Christmas Eve 2018 harmonic infrasound
disagreements.support: The earlier study used two time windows; this study inverts a continuous time series at higher temporal resolution.
disagreements.quote: Watson et al.20 focused on two time windows (before and after the flank eruption) and hence does not have the same temporal resolution

disagreements.target: Johnson et al. Cotopaxi approach to estimating crater air temperature from peak frequency and quality factor
disagreements.support: The authors argue the approach does not extend to complex geometries or variable temperature, and assume a constant temperature instead.
disagreements.quote: it is unclear how this approach can be applied to complex crater geometries or a spatially variable temperature profile

disagreements.target: Previous studies showing topographic scattering of local infrasound
disagreements.support: Peak frequency is consistent across stations, so topography is argued to be second-order below 3 Hz.
disagreements.quote: the remarkable consistency in peak frequency observations here indicates that topographic effects are a second-order influence

disagreements.target: Reports of infrasonic spectral shifts at Arenal, Pu`u `Ō`ō and Tungurahua
disagreements.support: The authors note those shifts were brief, tied to single explosions, or bidirectional, unlike the sustained monotonic glide at Etna.
disagreements.quote: however they entailed only a brief duration, occurred before or after single explosions

disagreements.target: Studies using an infrasound quality factor in depth or temperature analysis
disagreements.support: Large frequency changes within a deep conduit are argued to make the quality factor unnecessary here.
disagreements.quote: the analysis does not require incorporation of an infrasound quality factor used in other studies19,28

alternatives_considered.chosen: CRes quasi-1D numerical crater resonance model
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Cylindrical pipe Eq. (1); analytical exponential or Bessel horn solutions; 1D and 3D numerical models
alternatives_considered.reason: SEC geometry is not easily characterized by an analytical expression; CRes is a good predictor for relatively narrow conduits

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Spatially variable and changing temperature profile; temperature estimated from the quality factor (Johnson et al.)
alternatives_considered.reason: A varying profile has minimal impact on peak frequency (Watson et al.); the quality-factor approach is unclear for complex geometry
The source function mainly affects overtones; the fundamental is relatively unaffected

alternatives_considered.chosen: Exclude phase 2 (00:00 to 06:00, 20 February) from the analysis
alternatives_considered.reason: To avoid misinterpreting the low-frequency microbarom as volcanic signal

alternatives_considered.chosen: Five stations (ECPN, EMFO, EMFS, EMNR, ESLN)
DEM aligned to the 2014 DEM using the unchanged BN southern flank
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Evenly spread ground control points; UAS GPS georeferencing
alternatives_considered.reason: Ground control points are impossible on an active volcano; UAS GPS uncertainty exceeds 50 m on steep slopes

alternatives_considered.chosen: UAS survey for the inner crater geometry
North-south transect (b-b') for the quasi-1D geometry
alternatives_considered.reason: Comparison with 18 and 23 February satellite images, given the post-episode SE breach
